newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Only .007% of world's water said usable by humans.
newsitem.headline: Only .007% of world's water said usable by humans.

text.p: Water, water everywhere, but only about 0.007 percent of it is readily accessible for human use, according to a new U.N. report on that vital but fast depleting resource.
"Many people have an image of the world as a blue planet, for 70 percent of it is covered with water," said the report, prepared for the U.N. Commission on Sustainable Development.

"The reality is that 97.5 percent of all water on Earth is salt water, leaving only 2.5 percent as freshwater. Nearly 70 percent of that freshwater is frozen in the ice caps of Antarctica and Greenland, and most of the remainder is present as soil moisture, or lies in deep underground aquifers as groundwater not accessible to human use."

As a result, the report said, "less than one percent of the world's freshwater, or about 0.007 percent of all water on Earth, is readily accessible for direct human uses." This is the water found in lakes, rivers, reservoirs and underground sources shallow enough to be tapped at an affordable cost.
"Only this amount is regularly renewed by rain and snowfall, and therefore available on a sustainable basis."
The report said water use had been growing at more than twice the rate of the population increase during this century and already a number of regions were chonically water-short.
About a third of the world's population lived in countries experiencing moderate-to-high water stress partly resulting from increasing demands from a growing population and human activities, it said.
"By the year 2025, as much as two-thirds of the world population could be under stress conditions," the report said.
Water shortages and pollution were causing widespread public health problems, limiting economic and agricultural development and harming a wide range of ecosystems, it said.
"They may put global food supplies in jeopardy and lead to economic stagnation in many areas of the world. The result could be a series of local and regional water crises with global implications."

While in some cases action had been taken to reduce demand and pollution, thus relieving water stress, "far more widespread and sustained action is essential to reverse many of the unsustainable trends," the report cautioned.
Among factors that could make water problems worse unless action was taken was a projected increase in the world's population from 5.7 billion now to some 8.3 billion by 2025.

Another driving force would be increasing consumption of food and industrial goods produced using water, with irrigation already accounting for 70 percent of the water taken from lakes, rivers and underground sources.

"Because of increasing competition among demands for a finite resource, there is already a growing perception of water as an economic good and as a tradable commodity. As human demands grow, so will the price of water and possibly food prices, placing a heavier burden on the poorer strata of the world's population," the report said.

"Countries, often working in regional groups and with international institutions such as the United Nations, need to develop a broad range of water strategies based on the best information available."

Discussing various technologies for reducing water use, the report said that in some countries waste water was already being treated and used for irrigation. A number of industries had developed or adopted water management techniques abd technologies that greatly reduce water use.
